paras: The shooting of Allen and Alex Philips took place on Sunday afternoon, 12 June 1881, when a deputy sheriff's party trying to arrest Allen Philips, a Black man, shot both brothers at Alex's house on Dr. Huguet's plantation below Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Both men were wounded, and a physician judged the wounds not fatal. The Baton Rouge Louisiana Capitolian reported the officers' version in full and declared them "fully justified," and the story reached other Louisiana papers as a one-line exchange item.

According to the Capitolian, Allen Philips had been sentenced in the parish's district court for burglary and larceny and had escaped from the parish jail in 1876. On the morning of the shooting he was at John Wax's store at the southern edge of town, where, the paper said, he flourished a pistol and made threats until Wax disarmed him and sent him home. Chief T. B. Hillen identified him and told Sheriff J. W. Bates, who sent Deputy Sheriff Skolfield with Dennis Daigre as assistant and Henry Adams as identifier to serve a warrant.

The officers found the two brothers sitting near Alex Philips's house, and in their account both men "at once resisted arrest." Alex was said to have rushed Skolfield with a hoe, and Daigre shot him down. Allen, by the same account, took a butcher knife from a small child and rushed toward Skolfield and the house, and Skolfield and Daigre fired at him together at close range, both shots striking him.

Dr. Duchein visited the wounded brothers with Sheriff Bates the next day and judged their wounds not fatal if they received proper care, which the sheriff was said to be arranging. The sheriff then reported that Allen Philips had nearly beaten a white man to death at Plaquemine months earlier, and the paper added that an "Albert Philips" had threatened a store clerk with a pistol at Musson station. No report of either man's recovery or death, of charges against them, or of any inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

The Capitolian ran the story on 14 June under the headline "RESISTING ARREST. FATAL RESULT.," although its own text said the wounds were not considered fatal. Every detail came from the officers' side: the paper called the brothers "desperadoes" and "an annoyance and terror to the colored people of the neighborhood," and claimed that "a feeling of relief" pervaded the Black community. Two days later it printed a correction at Wax's request saying that Philips had misbehaved because Wax refused to sell him liquor, not because he had become drunk at the store, and the weekly edition of 18 June repeated both items.

Outside Baton Rouge, the Richland Beacon of Rayville reduced the affair to one sentence in its column of state exchanges on 25 June. Its version said the sheriff "went with a posse," that the brothers "resisted the officers," and that both were "dangerously wounded," without naming the officers or giving the accusations. No account from the Philips brothers or other Black residents appears in the coverage.

The papers differ on the severity of the wounds: the Capitolian's headline said "FATAL RESULT," its text cited Dr. Duchein's view that they were not fatal, and the Beacon called them dangerous. The local Capitolian, which named a deputy, an assistant and an identifier, is more specific than the Beacon's secondhand reference to the sheriff and "a posse."

reader.title: Shooting of Allen and Alex Philips
bases: A deputy sheriff and his assistant, sent with a warrant, shot both brothers while trying to arrest Allen Philips, an escaped prisoner (A1); the Beacon's 'posse' is a secondhand label for the same arrest party (A7).

Every detailed account comes from the Baton Rouge Capitolian (A1, A2, repeated in A4-A6); the Beacon's one-line brief (A7) appeared in its column of state exchanges and adds nothing independent beyond calling the wounds 'dangerous'.

accounts.gist: The brothers resisted arrest; Alex rushed Skolfield with a hoe and was shot by Daigre, then Allen took a butcher knife from a child and rushed Skolfield, and both officers shot him.

accounts.label: Storekeeper's correction
accounts.gist: Wax said Allen Philips misbehaved at his store because Wax refused to sell him liquor, not because he had become drunk there.

accounts.label: Exchange brief
accounts.gist: The sheriff of East Baton Rouge and a posse went to arrest Allen Philips; he and his brother resisted and both were shot and dangerously wounded.

framing.detail: Headlined 'RESISTING ARREST. FATAL RESULT.', the Capitolian called the brothers 'desperadoes' and a 'terror to the colored people' and judged the officers 'fully justified'.
The Richland Beacon gave the shooting one sentence among state exchanges, adopting the officers' 'resisted' without comment.
